title: Conduct continuous hazard identification and risk assessment within a workplace

lessons.title: Why we assess risk and how to prepare
lessons.html:
The legal requirement

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires employers to identify hazards, assess the risks and put measures in place to control them, as far as is reasonably practicable. Workers must cooperate and report hazards. This is called hazard identification and risk assessment (HIRA).

Continuous HIRA means it is not a once-a-year paper exercise. It is done before each task, when conditions change, after an incident, and as part of daily work. A spray team, for example, checks the wind and the area each morning before they start.

Key words

  • Hazard: anything with the potential to cause harm, such as a chemical, a moving shaft, a bull, a slippery floor.
  • Risk: the chance that the hazard will cause harm, combined with how serious the harm would be.
  • Control: a measure that removes the hazard or lowers the risk.

Preparing for hazard identification

  1. Know the area and the task: what work is done, by whom, with what equipment and substances.
  2. Get the tools: a checklist or HIRA form, pen, the previous assessment, incident records, and the safe work procedures.
  3. Wear the PPE needed for the area.
  4. Tell the supervisor of the area that you are coming, and talk to the workers who do the job. They know where the problems are.
  5. Plan the route so you see every part of the task, including start-up, cleaning and maintenance, not only normal work.

Look for hazards in all groups: mechanical, electrical, chemical, biological (animals, zoonoses), physical (noise, heat, sun), ergonomic (lifting, repetitive work), fire, and people factors such as fatigue or lack of training.

lessons.title: Assessing risk and taking action
lessons.html:
Identifying hazards

Walk through the task step by step. For each step, ask: what can go wrong, who can be hurt, and how? Write down each hazard clearly, for example: auger in the feed mill has no guard on the intake; worker's hand could be caught.

Rating the risk

Many workplaces use a simple matrix: likelihood multiplied by severity.

LikelihoodSeverityRisk
Unlikely (1)Minor injury (1)1 Low
Possible (2)Lost-time injury (2)4 Medium
Likely (3)Fatal or permanent injury (3)9 High

High risks need action before work continues. Follow your workplace's own matrix if it uses different numbers.

Choosing controls: the hierarchy

  1. Eliminate the hazard (stop using it).
  2. Substitute it with something safer (a less toxic chemical).
  3. Engineering controls: guards, barriers, ventilation.
  4. Administrative controls: procedures, training, signs, job rotation.
  5. PPE: gloves, goggles, respirators. PPE is the last line of defence.

Remedial and follow-up action

  • Stop the work and make the area safe if there is an immediate danger.
  • Report findings to your supervisor and the health and safety representative, in writing.
  • Record what action is needed, who is responsible and by when.
  • Check later that the action was done and that it worked.
  • Update the risk assessment and tell the workers about the changes.

Key points

  • The OHS Act requires hazards to be identified and risks controlled.
  • HIRA is continuous: before tasks, when things change and after incidents.
  • Risk combines likelihood and severity.
  • Use the hierarchy of controls; PPE is the last option.
  • Record actions, assign responsibility and follow up.
